paragraphs: This is the root of the ancient word, here in this place called Quiche. Here we shall write, here we shall begin the ancient word, the root and the start of everything that was done in the citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people. And here we shall bring out its being shown, its being made plain, its being told — the hiding, the making clear — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Mother and Father, whose names are Hun Ahpu Vuch, Hun Ahpu Vtiu, Great White Coati, Tepeu, Gucumatz, the Heart of the Lake, the Heart of the Sea, He of the Green Plate, He of the Green Gourd, so they are called; and named along with them, spoken of along with them, the grandmother and the grandfather, whose names are Xpiyacoc and Xmucane, protector and shelterer, twice a midwife, twice a grandfather, as they are named in the Quiche word — when they told, when they gave account of all that they did together, within the clarity that had already come to be, within the words that had already come to be told.

This we shall write now within the word of God, within Christianity; we bring it out because there is no longer a place to see it, the ancient book, the original writing whose sight is hidden from the one who looks at it, from the one who ponders it. Great is its telling and its account of when the sky and the earth were finished being formed, squared, divided into four parts, measured out, when the cord was stretched across the sky and across the earth, its four corners, its four sides, as it is told — by the one who builds, the one who gives shape, mother and father of life and of what was made, who gives breath, who gives thought, who watches over the good walk of the people, of humankind, born into clarity, begotten into clarity, one who worries over, one who knows all that lies within the sky, the earth, the lake, the sea.

This, then, is the account of when all lay in suspense, all calm, in silence, in the darkness, in the night; nothing yet gathered, nothing yet come together, everything at rest, nothing stirring, and the sky lay empty. This is the first word, the first speech. There was not yet one person, one animal, bird, fish, crab, tree, stone, hollow, canyon, meadow, forest. Only the sky existed. The face of the earth had not yet appeared. Only the sea lay penned in, alone, and all that was of the sky. Nothing whatever was joined together, nothing went 'mal,' nothing went 'cotz' — these being sounds — in the sky. Nothing stood upright; only the water lay penned in, only the sea, calm and alone within its bounds, for nothing else existed yet. Only stillness and silence in the darkness, in the night. Only the one who builds, the one who gives shape, Tepeu, Gucumatz, Mother, Father, lay in the water, surrounded by clarity, hidden under green and blue feathers — and so they are called Gucumatz. Great sages, great thinkers were they in their being; and so it was that the sky existed, and the Heart of the Sky existed too, for that is the name of this god, as it is told.

Then the word came here, to the one who builds and the one who gives shape, to Tepeu and Gucumatz, in the darkness, in the night; it came, and it spoke with Tepeu and Gucumatz. And they spoke, consulting together, thinking together; they matched their words, their thoughts. Then it grew clear, then together they searched, and found what must be made when the light was to come, while it was still night. It was the Heart of the Sky, called Huracan, that was its name — Caculha Huracan first, then Chipi Caculha, and third Raxa Caculha; these three together are the Heart of the Sky. They came together, then, with Tepeu and Gucumatz, and there the light and the life were thought upon: how the sowing would be done, how the dawn would be brought forth, who would provide, who would sustain.

"Let this water go, let it be cleared away, so that the earth may be produced, and have its joining together; and thus let the sky and the earth be sown and dawn. And so it will not be an obstacle to the creatures, to what we make, when men are made," they said, before the earth was created by them.

"Earth," they said, and at once it was made. Like a mist, like a cloud was its forming, taking shape, when the hills appeared out of the water like a crab rising up; and in an instant the great mountains came to be. Only by a wonder, only by an act of power, was this done, this forming of the cypresses and the pines upon its face. And so Gucumatz rejoiced: "Good is your coming, Heart of Sky, you Huracan, and you Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha; our work, our making, will be brought to completion," they said. First the earth was made, the hills and the flatlands; the courses of the water were divided, and the streams went their way among the hills, and the water stood apart when the great mountains appeared. Thus was the making of the earth, when it was made by the Heart of Sky, the Heart of Earth, as they are called who first made fruitful the sky and made fruitful also the earth within the water, when they gave it thought, when they gave it consideration, and brought their work to its completion.

candidate.translator_note: Round-5 revision responding to reviewer feedback on two points. First, the section was found to end prematurely at the command to clear the water, omitting the entire earth-creation narrative present in the K'iche'/Spanish: the earth spoken into being ("Earth!" and it was made at once), its forming like mist and cloud, the hills rising from the water like a crab, the instant appearance of great mountains, the growth of cypresses and pines upon its face, Gucumatz's joyful address to Heart of Sky/Huracan/Chipi Caculha/Raxa Caculha, the dividing of the water-courses among the hills, and the closing summary naming Heart of Sky and Heart of Earth together as the earth's makers. This is now restored as a new closing paragraph, translated directly from the K'iche' (with the Spanish, which is fuller here, consulted as an aid). Second, the closing command was found to echo Recinos's and Goetz & Morley's distinctive "neither glory nor grandeur... until the human being is made" wording, which is not required by the source; Ximenez's own gloss reads the passage as the cleared water not being embarazo (an obstacle, an encumbrance) to the creatures still to come, so the command is now rendered plainly along those lines — the water withdrawing so it will "not be an obstacle to the creatures, to what we make, when men are made" — dropping the invented glory/grandeur clause entirely rather than reaching for a different translator's phrasing of it.

last_review.resemblance_note: The opening paragraph clusters several of Dennis Tedlock's distinctive interpretive choices: "here in this place called Quiche" (Tedlock's exact opening phrase; the K'iche' "varal Quiche vbi" is literally just "here, Quiche its name" — Ximenez glosses "aqui en el quiche", Christenson has "this place called Quiché" differently framed), and especially "in the citadel of Quiche, in the nation of the Quiche people" — rendering "tinamit" as "citadel" is a hallmark Tedlock choice (Ximenez glosses it "pueblo"; Recinos/Goetz-Morley have "town/country"), and the paired phrase matches Tedlock's "everything done in the citadel of Quiché, in the nation of Quiché people" nearly verbatim. Individually forced-ish renderings elsewhere ("Heart of Sky," "the sowing/the dawn," "midwife... grandfather") are fine, but this opening cluster should be reworded (e.g. "in the town of Quiche, among the Quiche people").
last_review.issues: Fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph: the previously missing earth-creation ending is now present and tracks the K'iche'/Spanish (Earth spoken into being, mist/cloud forming, crab simile, mountains, cypresses and pines, Gucumatz's rejoicing, water-courses dividing, Heart of Sky/Heart of Earth closing). Minor quibbles only: "twice a midwife, twice a grandfather" — source has "camul yiom, camul mamom" (twice midwife, twice patriarch/grandfather), fine; "protector and shelterer" for matzanel chuquenel is defensible (Ximenez: amparadores y cubridores). "Ilbal zac petenac chaca palo" ("the instrument of sight that came from across the sea") is compressed to "no longer a place to see it, the ancient book" — the across-the-sea provenance clause is dropped, a real omission though small. title: Jun Junajpu, Wuqub' Junajpu, and their sons Jun B'atz'/Jun Chowen

paragraphs: Now the third who grew proud was Cabracan, the second son of Vucub Caquix — whose name means, as the manuscript itself glosses it, "of two legs." "I am the one who tears down the mountains," he said. But Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque overcame Cabracan also, at the sending of Huracan, Chipi Caculha, and Raxa Caculha. "Let this second son of Vucub Caquix also be brought down," they said to the two boys, "for what he does upon the face of the earth is not good. He reaches beyond his measure, and it must not be so. Draw him out and lead him to where the sun rises." So spoke Huracan to the two boys. "It is well," they answered, "for what we see is not right. Are you not first, O Heart of the Sky?" So the boys replied to what Huracan had told them. Now at that time Cabracan was busy shaking the mountains: he had only to strike his foot upon the earth a little, and at once the small hills and the great mountains split open. The two boys came upon him and asked him, "Where are you going, boy?" "Nowhere," he said. "I am only here knocking down mountains, and so I will go on doing forever." Then Cabracan said to Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque, "What is it you have come for? I do not know your faces — what are your names?" "We have no name," they said. "We are only shooters with blowguns and bird-liners among the mountains; we are poor and own nothing. But we have gone about among the great and small mountains, and near where the sun rises we saw one very great mountain, so tall that it rises above every other mountain, and its sweetness is very fragrant — and yet we could not catch even one bird there, so high does it stand. Is it true, as they say, that you can bring down every mountain?" So Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque spoke to Cabracan. "Is that true? Where is this mountain you speak of? I will see it and knock it flat. Where did you see it?" "Over there," they said, "where the sun rises." "Good," said Cabracan, "lead the way." "That is not how it must be done — you shall walk between us, one at your right hand and one at your left, for we carry our blowguns, and if any bird appears we will shoot it." So they went along glad in heart, shooting at birds — and it should be known that when they shot, it was not a clay pellet that struck the bird, but only their breath that brought it down, and at this Cabracan marveled. Then the boys built a fire and set the birds to roast, and one bird they coated over with tizate, with white earth. "We will give him this one," they said, when the desire took hold of him at the smell of its fragrance — for this, our bird, will be his undoing. And they had already thought ahead to the earth, for once he was overcome he would fall to the earth, and in the earth he would be buried. Truly he is a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being, when the planting is done, when the dawn is born — so the boys said among themselves, for it was only in their own hearts that this device was carried and worked out; in just this way Cabracan's heart was to be overcome, said Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque to one another. Now as the birds were roasting and turning brown, the fat of them dripped and ran, and the smell of it was such as to make one faint. Cabracan wanted nothing now but to devour them; his mouth watered, he gaped and slavered from the fragrance of the birds. Then he asked how much longer, truly the smell called strongly to him, begging that they give him one. And so they gave Cabracan the bird, the one prepared for his defeat, and when he had swallowed it they set out again and came at last to where the sun rises, where the great mountain stood.

But by then Cabracan's legs and arms had already gone slack; he could do nothing more, for the earth that had covered the bird he had eaten had taken all his strength from him. Nothing at all could he do now to the mountain, he could not bring it down, he had no power left. Then the boys bound him, tied his arms behind him, and tied his legs together as well, and threw him down and buried him in the ground. In this way Cabracan was overcome by Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque alone. Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth. Now we shall tell also of the birth of Hun Ahpu and Xbalanque; only first, only in part, have we told of the overcoming of Vucub Caquix, together with Zipacna and Cabracan, here upon the face of the earth. Now we shall also tell the name of their father — but only in part shall it be told, only a portion of the account of their father's name is given here.

candidate.translator_note: Round-4 fix. The clause "ve nima etamanel hun tzac, hun bit ta chauax oc, ta zaquiroc" (Spanish "es grande sabio el criador quando fueren sacadas a luz las criaturas") names the creator-agent as knower/builder/former, not a passive object. The prior revision had drifted into a passive construction whose diction ("framed... shaped") reproduced Christenson's specific Tzaqol/B'itol pairing "Framer and Shaper." This version restores the active, agentive sense — "a great knower, the builder, the one who raises things and gives them their being" — worked independently from the K'iche' root senses (tzac: to build/erect; bit: to give form/bring into being) and from the Spanish "criador," deliberately avoiding both Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" pairs. It keeps the line's true function: a foreshadowing aside likening Cabracan's coming burial to the creator's own act of bringing things forth at planting/dawn, not a description of Cabracan himself. The passage's proper-name spellings (Vucub Caquix, Cabracan, Chipi Caculha, Raxa Caculha) and "Heart of the Sky" were reviewed as close to manuscript orthography/minor variants and left as is, per the audit's own assessment that they are defensible. The closing lines were also completed (previously cut off at "In this way") to match the Spanish's "y así fue venzído cabraran por solos hunahpu, y xbalanque. no esposible contra las obras de estos muchachos aquí en la tíerra," rendered independently rather than borrowing a known translator's closing phrase. Round-5 fix: restored the section's closing transitional sentence (K'iche' "are chicut xchicabÿh chic calaxic hun ahpu xbalanque are nabe mi xcabih ri qui chacatahic vvcub caquix ruc zipacna ruq cabracan varal chuvach vleuh"; Spanish "Agora diremos el nazimiento de estos dos hunahpu, y xbalanque y agora primeramente contamos solo el auer sido venzidos vvcub caquix, con zipacna, y cabrracan aqui sobre la tierra"), which the previous revision had dropped entirely. Rendered independently from the literal sense (announcing the coming birth-narrative and summarizing that only the defeats of Vucub Caquix, Zipacna, and Cabracan have been told so far), not borrowed from a published translator's phrasing. The K'iche' text's further clause naming the fathers ("are chicut xchicabÿh chic vbi qui cahau...") belongs to the following section (s09), which already opens with "Now we shall tell the name of the father," so it is left there rather than duplicated here. Round-6 fix: replaced the interpolated gloss "his name means 'earthquake'" with the manuscript's own parenthetical gloss (Spanish "esto es de dos piernas"), rendered as "of two legs," attributed explicitly to the source rather than presented as an unmarked scholarly identification. Also restored the section's final transitional clause naming the forthcoming account of the fathers (K'iche' "...xa nicah xchicabÿh, xa chacab v bixic quicahau"; Spanish sense: the telling is given only in part/by half), translated independently as "only in part shall it be told, only a portion of the account of their father's name is given here" — this duplicates in sense, not wording, the opening of s09, since the K'iche' transition itself straddles the two sections.

last_review.issues: 1) OMISSION (main problem): the K'iche' source ends with a transitional coda after Cabracan's burial: "Are chicut xchicabÿh chic calaxic hun ahpu xbalanque... are nabe mi xcabih ri qui chacatahic vvcub caquix, ruc zipacna, ruq cabracan... Are chicut xchicabÿh chic v bi qui cahau... xa nicah xchicabÿh, xa chacab v bixic quicahau" (Spanish: "Agora diremos el nazimiento de estos dos hunahpu, y xbalanque y agora primeramente contamos solo el auer sido venzidos vvcub caquix, con zipacna, y cabrracan aqui sobre la tierra"). This announces the coming account of the heroes' birth and of the names of their fathers — the very subject of the section title — and says it will be told "only half / in part." The candidate stops at "Nothing could stand against what these two did here upon the face of the earth" and omits this entire transition, even though the translator_note claims the closing lines were completed; only the "y asi fue venzido" sentence was restored, not the "Agora diremos el nazimiento" coda. 2) Minor: the opening gloss "his name means 'earthquake'" is an interpolation; the manuscript's own parenthetical gloss is "esto es de dos piernas" (two-legs). "Earthquake" is the standard scholarly identification (Recinos/Tedlock render the name as Earthquake), so it is not a distinctive borrowing, but it silently replaces the source's own gloss and should either follow the source or be marked editorial. Otherwise the fidelity is good paragraph by paragraph (blowgun/birdlime hunters, breath-shot birds, tizate/white-earth bird, weakened limbs, binding and burial all carried), and the creator-aside now avoids Tedlock's "Maker, Modeler" and Christenson's "Framer, Shaper" and their "sowing/dawning" formula ("when the planting is done, when the dawn is born" is close in sense but not their wording). Proper-name spellings follow manuscript orthography as previously accepted.

"Earthquake" as a gloss is common scholarly identification, not a distinctive phrase.

title: The Xibalba trial-houses and the death of the elder twins

paragraphs: Then Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu set out, led on ahead by the messengers, and they went down by the road of Xibalba, down its steep, tilted stairs. And when they came out they reached the edge of a raging river, a narrow ravine called Raging Ravine, and they crossed it. Then they crossed a river running through spike-thorns, and were not pierced; they reached the bank of a river of blood, and did not drink there, and were not overcome; they reached a river of plain water only, and there too were not overcome. And going on further they came to where the road forks into four.

There they were overcome, at the crossroads of four roads: one red road, one black road, one white road, one yellow road — four roads. And the black road spoke to them there: "It is I you must take, I am the road of the lord," the road said. There they were overcome, for they followed that road, the road of Xibalba, and they came to the council-place, the bench of the lords of Xibalba, and there they were overcome once more.

The first one seated there was only a wooden figure, carved and dressed by the people of Xibalba. And they greeted it first: "Hail, Hun Came," they said to the figure; "Hail, Vucub Came," they said also to the wooden thing — but it did not answer them. Then the lords of Xibalba burst into great laughter, all the lords laughed greatly together, for in their hearts they had already won against Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu; they laughed.

Then Hun Came and Vucub Came spoke again: "Good, you have come. Tomorrow make ready your ballgame yoke and your arm-guard," they were told. "Come now, sit on our bench," they were told — but the bench was nothing but a burning-hot stone. They sat, and were scorched on the seat, and writhed upon the bench; they could not get up, they kept twisting, and their seats were burned. Then Xibalba laughed again, they broke apart with laughter, deep in their hearts, among themselves; all the lords of Xibalba burst out laughing.

"Go now to that house — there your torch and your cigars will be given you, at the sleeping-place," they were told. Then they arrived at the House of Blackness, where there was only darkness within. Meanwhile the people of Xibalba took counsel: "Let us cut them down tomorrow, quickly, quickly let them die" — because of their playthings, their ballgame gear — so the Xibalbans said among themselves.

Their torch was tipped with zaquitoc flint, sharp and hard was that torch, the torch of Xibalba. And Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu went into the House of Blackness. Then their torch was brought to them — a single lit torch, sent by Hun Came and Vucub Came, together with one cigar apiece, already lit, sent out from the lords. When it was carried in to Hunhunahpu and Vucub Hunahpu, they were huddled there in the darkness, and when the bearer of the torch and the cigars arrived, the torch came in shining. paragraphs: Here now it is told of a maiden, daughter of a lord called Kuchumakik. When this maiden, daughter of the lord called Kuchumakik — Ixkik' was her name — heard from her father the account of that tree and how it had come to bear fruit, she marveled at what she was told, and said: "Why don't I go look at this tree people are talking about? Surely its fruit is good to taste, from what they say and what I hear." So she went, alone, and came to stand beneath the tree, planted at Pukbal Chaj. "What beautiful fruit! How beautifully this tree bears!" she said. "Will nothing happen to me if I pick one of these?" Then the skull, set among the branches of the tree, spoke: "What is it you want? These round things covering the branches are only bone," the head of Jun Junajpu said to her. "Is that truly what you want?" it asked her. "Yes, I want it," the maiden answered. "Very well. Stretch out your right hand here, so I may see it," said the skull. "Yes," said the maiden, and she raised her right hand, up before the skull. Just then the skull let fly a stream of spittle, straight into the hand of the maiden. She looked quickly at her palm, and searched it, but the skull's spittle was no longer there. "In my saliva and my spittle I have given you my line," the skull said. "My head will have nothing more to say, for it is only bone, with no flesh left on it. Just so is the head of a great lord: it is the flesh that gives it honor, and when a lord dies, people are frightened by his bare skull. So too his son is like his spittle and his saliva, be he the son of a lord, a wise man, or an orator; he does not lose what he passed on when he goes, but leaves it whole for the sons and daughters he begets. So I have done with you. Now climb up there, to the face of the earth; you will not die. Hold fast to what I have spoken." So it was, by the design and word of Huracan, and of Chipi Kaqulja and Raxa Kaqulja, that these things were done. Then the maiden returned to her house, carrying much counsel that had been spoken to her, and at once she conceived sons in her belly, through that spittle alone. And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived.

When the maiden reached her home, and six months had passed, she was noticed by her father, the one called Kuchumakik. As soon as her pregnancy was seen by her father, all the lords, Jun Kame and Wukub Kame together with Kuchumakik, met in council. "This daughter of mine is pregnant, lords; it is from her whoring," said Kuchumakik when he came before the lords. "Very well," they said. "Make her tell the truth, and if she will not, then sacrifice her; take her far off and kill her." "Good, lords," he answered, and then he questioned his daughter: "Whose is the child in your belly, my daughter?" She said: "I have no child, my father; I have not yet known the face of any man." "Very well," he said. "You are indeed a whore. Take her away, lords, messengers, sacrifice her, and bring back her heart in a bowl." This was told to the owls, who were four. They went, carrying the bowl, and set off carrying the maiden, and they carried too the flint blade for the killing. Then she said to them: "You must not kill me, messengers, for what I carry in my belly is no wrongdoing — it came about of itself, when I went to marvel at the head of Jun Junajpu, at Pukbal Chaj. So you must not kill me, messengers," the maiden told them.

"What then shall we put in place of your heart? Your father told us: bring back her heart in the bowl. Report back to the lords, do not fail us, or else we too must die. Is there not something we might carry in truth?" "Very well," she answered. "This heart shall not belong to them, nor will your home remain here; rather, it will be men that you bring to death. And truly that shall be your nature: to be deceivers. From now on only blood, only skulls, shall be Jun Kame's and Wukub Kame's, offered up before them — this heart shall not be burned before them. Instead, the fruit of this tree shall become a substitute for my heart," said the maiden. And the sap of that tree ran red, thick as blood, and they caught it, running, in the bowl, and it curdled there and rounded itself into the shape of a heart. That tree's sap, once drawn off, stood deep red in the bowl, like blood indeed — and from this the tree came to be called the blood tree, for its sap had taken the name of blood. "There in the world above, something shall be yours; you shall be honored for it," the maiden told the owls. "Very well, maiden," they answered her. "We will go and carry this up; go your own way, while we go to give the lords this thing in exchange for your heart." So the messengers said. And when they came before the lords, who were all waiting, "Is it done, then?" said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. "It is done, lords. Here is her heart, in the bottom of this bowl." "Good — let us see it," said Jun Kame and Wukub Kame; and taking it up between three fingers, they lifted it, and it dripped with what seemed blood, deep red. "Stir up the fire well, and set it upon the coals," said Jun Kame. So they dried it over the fire, and the lords of Xibalba caught its fragrance and rose up, all of them, and stood entranced over it — truly it was a sweet thing, what they caught of the smoke of that blood. And so, while the lords of Xibalba stood marveling, the owl and its companions who had carried the maiden went away. Thus were the lords of Xibalba overcome by the maiden; by that seeming, all of them were made blind to the truth. The maiden's guides left her there, at the hole so named in the earth, and turned back up into the sky — thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it. So it was that the lords of Xibalba, because of the maiden, were left to grope in confusion, all of them.

candidate.translator_note: Round 5 revision, addressing round-4 audit. (1) "pucbal chah," the tree's location, is no longer rendered "Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice" — that etymological gloss is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive coinage and is not required by the source: Ximénez's Spanish treats the spot plainly as the place where ashes were thrown ("donde echaban la zeniza"), and Recinos simply keeps it as the proper name Pucbal-Chah. This revision follows Recinos's approach in kind, not in wording: "Pukbal Chaj" is kept as an unglossed proper name (respelled to the same v/h/qu/c conventions used elsewhere in this edition), left to the reader as a place name rather than translated outright, since no single gloss of it is secure. (2) paragraphs[0] previously closed with a garbled, self-contradicting clause ("Jun Junajpu's namesake and Xbalanke conceived — Junajpu and Xbalanke"); it now ends, consistent with full_text, "And so were Junajpu and Xbalanke conceived." (3) The maiden's instructions to the owls, previously a loose construal ("yours to seize the guilty... honored warriors"), is now translated closer to the literal K'iche'/Spanish: she tells them the heart demanded of her is not truly owed to Xibalba, that the owls' home and work from now on lie among the living rather than in the underworld, that their nature will be to deceive, and that only blood and skulls — not a true heart — belong to Jun Kame and Wukub Kame. Names retain the independent, unhyphenated respelling from the prior round (Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Jun Junajpu, Xbalanke, Chipi Kaqulja, Raxa Kaqulja), tracking neither Recinos's colonial spelling nor Christenson's practical orthography wholesale; Ixkik' is unchanged. "xzalih chicu cah oc ri vabanel" remains genuinely difficult and is still offered as a hedged, plain construal ("thus, it seems, becoming watchers over it") rather than a confident equivalence with any specific mythological office. Round 6: restored the maiden's admiring exclamation under the tree ("what beautiful fruit and how beautifully this tree bears" — Ximénez "que hermoso fruto y que hermosamente fructifica este arbol"), which had been dropped from paragraph 1; re-checked the owls'-prophecy passage against Ximénez's Spanish ("haréis fuerza a los hombres que mueran... vuestro ser será ser engañadores") and confirmed the existing wording already tracks it (men brought to death, the owls' nature to be deceivers, only blood and skulls belonging to Jun Kame and Wukub Kame).

last_review.resemblance_note: "The Place of Ball-Game Sacrifice" (twice, for "pucbal chah") is Dennis Tedlock's distinctive etymological rendering. It is not forced by the source: Ximénez glosses the spot simply as the ash-dumping place ("enfrente de donde echaban la ceniza"), Recinos leaves the place-name untranslated (Pucbal-Chah), and Christenson renders it "Crushing Ballcourt." Recommend a neutral alternative (e.g., leaving "Pukbal Chaj" as a name, or "the ash heap"). The proper-name respellings themselves (Kuchumakik, Jun Kame, Wukub Kame, Xbalanke, Chipi/Raxa Kaqulja) are independent and no longer track any one published system.

paragraphs: "We are going, grandmother. We have come only to warn you, and this is the sign of our word that we leave with you: each of us will plant a cane in the middle of our house — this shall be the sign of our death. If it dries, say: 'They are dead, it seems.' But if it sprouts again, say: 'They are alive.' Grandmother, and you, mother, do not weep — this sign remains with you as our word." And when they went, one Hunahpu planted, and the other Xbalanque planted; and they planted them only inside the house, not on the mountain, nor in wet ground, but in dry ground, in the middle of the house they left them planted.

Then they went, each carrying his own blowgun, and they went down into Xibalba. Quickly they went down the steps, and they crossed a river running through a ravine, and they passed among the birds; these birds were called Molay. And they also crossed a river of pus, and another of blood, meant to defeat them, as those of Xibalba supposed — but they did not step in them. And going on from there, they came to a crossroads of four roads, and they truly knew the road of Xibalba: one was black, one white, one red, and one green. And from there they sent out a small creature, an insect called Xan, to go and gather news. It was told: bite each of them, one by one; bite the first who sits there first, and finish biting them all, and yours shall be the sucking of the people's blood on the roads. This was told to Xan. Very well, said Xan.

Then it took the black road and went straight to the first one seated there, who was a thing made of carved wood, dressed up; and it bit him first, and he did not speak. And then it bit the second, and he too did not speak. It bit the third, who was Hun Came, and he cried out — Ay! — when he was bitten. What is it, Hun Came, said the fourth seated there, who bit you? I don't know what has bitten me. It bit the next, and he cried, Ay, what is this, Vucub Came, who has bitten you? said the fifth. Ay, ay, said Xiquiripat. candidate.translator_note: Revised to fix four fidelity issues flagged in round-2 review, working from the K'iche' (with the Spanish as an aid). (1) The ball Xibalba proposes is now named as the source names it — "a worm, called chil" (Spanish "este gusanío, que se llama chíl"; K'iche' huchil) — rather than mistakenly reusing "Xan," which is the mosquito/gnat from the earlier road episode, a different creature entirely; "Xan" is now used only where the source itself uses it, in the crossroads scene. (2) The ants' summons is now given as direct speech inside the house of knives ("come, all knife-ants, all thigh-ants, come, all of you, go, and bring all the flowers we have promised to the lords" / "very well, said the ants"), matching "chai zanic, che que'n zanic, quixpetoc..." and the parallel Spanish "hormigas de navajas, hormigas de el muslo, venid...", instead of only mentioning the ants after the fact. (3) The named bird-guards are restored: Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu, with their cries transliterated ("xpurpuvec, xpurpuvec" / "puhuyu, puhuyu"), the lords' forewarning to watch the flowers all night, and the etiology of their manner of calling ("and from there came their manner of singing... so the two guards... are named Xpurpuvec and Puhuyu"), matching "de allí vino su modo de cantar" and the naming clause in the K'iche'; the later line about their mouths is kept tied to this same etiological pattern ("and from there came the shape of their mouths, slit in that fashion") rather than left as a vague aside. (4) The betting sequence is restored: the four gourds of flowers are now explicitly set as the wager on the game ("that was the wager they set upon the game"), the boys' willing self-defeat is rendered plainly ("it pleased their hearts to let themselves be defeated so"), and Xibalba's gloating is given as direct speech in the knife-house scene ("a good thing we have done... where now will they go to get flowers? this very night you must give us the flowers — we have beaten you"), matching "Buena cosa hemos hecho decían los de el infierno... ya os hemos ganado." House and object names remain plain literal renderings — "a black house," "house of knives," "white flint dagger," "head of a puma" — deliberately avoiding Tedlock's "Dark House," Goetz-Morley's "House of Gloom," and Christenson's coined equivalents.

title: Departure from Tulan; the long migration

paragraphs: So they came, all of them, to Tulan, and their numbers could not be counted — many were they who went, all in their file, when the gods came forth: first Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam. And they rejoiced, saying, "Now we have found what we were looking for." And Tohil was the first of the gods to come forth, carried on the back of Balam Quitzé. Then Avilix came forth, borne by Balam Acab. Then Hacavitz, borne by Mahucutah. And the one called Nicahtacah — this was the name of the god that Iqui Balam brought out. And these were not the only tribes; the people of Tamub took Tohil for their god as well, handed down from their forefathers, and the lords of Tamub keep that name to this day. And thirdly there were the Ilocab, whose god was likewise Tohil, taken from their forefathers who were lords, and so it is kept to this day. In this way the three branches of the Quiché were named, and none of them broke apart from the others, for the god of all was one and the same — Tohil to the Quiché, Tohil to the Tamub, Tohil to the Ilocab; one only was the name of their god, and so the three great branches of the Quiché did not divide from one another; Tohil, Avilix, Hacavitz — truly great was their standing. And then all the tribes entered in: the people of Rabinal, the Cakchiquel, those of Tziquinaha, and the people now called Yaqui. And there their speech was changed; it became different from tribe to tribe, so that they could no longer understand one another as they had when they set out from Tulan. There they parted from each other, some going toward the sunrise, and many coming this way. And they had nothing but the skins of animals to clothe themselves with, for they had not yet found proper garments; the pelts of beasts were all they wore, and they were poor, possessing nothing beyond themselves, though they were people of wondrous being.

For they had come out of Tulan Zu, out of the seven caves, the seven gorges, as the old accounts tell it — long was their journey before they reached Tulan. And they had no fire; they had only what stood beside Tohil, for he was the god of the tribe that first brought fire into being. And how he made it is not known — only that the fire was already blazing when Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam saw it. "Alas, we have no fire — we shall die of cold," they said. Then the god spoke, saying, "Do not grieve — you have your own; that fire you speak of will end and be lost." "Is that truly so?" they asked. "By your favor, you our god, our support and our sustenance are you, our god." And so they gave thanks for what he had said. And he answered, "It is well. Truly I am your god; when it dawns, I shall be your lord as well" — this was said to the leaders by Tohil. And so the tribes warmed themselves and rejoiced over the fire. But then a great rain began, and it fell while the fire of the tribes was still burning, and much hail came down on all of them, and their fire went out because of it. Then Balam Quitzé and Balam Acab asked again for their fire. "Our god, we are perishing of cold," they said to Tohil. "It is well," he said, "do not grieve." And then he brought the fire forth, turning it out from within his sandal, and Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam rejoiced, and warmed themselves once more.

Now the fire of the other tribes had gone out, and they were dying of cold. They came to beg fire of Balam Quitzé, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, for they could no longer bear the cold and the frost; they came shivering, their teeth chattering, and they seemed as good as dead, bent double, their feet and hands crippled, unable to grasp anything when they arrived. title: Wars, later kings, and the coming of the Spaniards

paragraphs: You there, beauty of this day, Huracan, heart of the sky and heart of the earth, giver of our glory and giver also of our sons and our daughters — turn back, bring your glory this way; let there be life, let my sons and my daughters be raised up, let them multiply, let them increase, they who feed and sustain you, they who call on you along the road, at the rivers, in the ravines, beneath the trees, beneath the vines; give them their sons and their daughters. Let no misfortune or disgrace find them, let them not be deceived, let them not stumble, let them not fornicate, let them not be judged before any tribunal, let them not go astray on the high side of the road or the low side of the road; let no blow fall on them before your face. Set them on a good road, a fair road. Let there be no misfortune, no disgrace upon their persons before your face, you heart of the sky, you heart of the earth, you bundle of glory, you Tohil, Auilix, Hacavitz, womb of sky, womb of earth, four corners. Let there be only peace before your face, you who are our god.' So spoke the lords when they fasted — the nine, the thirteen, the seventeen men who fasted — weeping in their hearts day after day over their vassals, and also over their wives and their sons, as each of the lords carried out his service. This was the price by which the dawn-light and life were bought, and the price too of the lordship — the rule of the ahpop, the ahpop camha, the elders, the principal men. Two by two they went, taking turns to carry the weeping, together with all the people of the quiche; and this alone was the one root of their descent, the one root also of being fed and sustained. So too did those of Tamub and Ilocab, together with those of Rabinal and the Cakchiquel, and those of Quiquinaha, Tuhalha, and Uchabaha; it was one and the same custom for all of them, as heard there among the quiche, done for the sake of everyone; not simply did they become lords in this way, nor did they merely set their hearts on eating and drinking alone. And not without cause did they subject them and seize the lordship and their greatness; nor was it for nothing that the towns of the small tribes and the great tribes were conquered. Great was the price given: jade was brought, silver was brought, quetzal feathers were brought, green feathers, and the tribute of all the peoples was already brought. This came before the sorcerer-lords Cucumatz and Cotuha, and before Quicab and Cavizimah as well, great lords of throne and house. Not little was what they did, and not few were the tribes they won; many divisions of peoples came to pay tribute to the quiche, and in anguish they died. Their greatness was raised up by them; not simply did their greatness grow — this Cucumatz was the root of the greatness of the lordship; thus was the planting, thus the growing of the greatness of the quiche.

Now we shall name the generations and orders of the lords together with all their names, we shall tell it again. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship of all the descendants of Balam Quitze, Balam Acab, Mahucutah, and Iqui Balam, our first grandfathers, our first fathers, at the time when the sun appeared, and the moon, and the stars. This, then, is the generations and orders of the lordship; here we shall set down the entering of the lords into office, as they entered, as they died, one after another, each one of the lords. This, then, shall be told of each and every one of the lords of the Quiché. Balam Quitze was the root of the house of the Cavek; his second was Cocavib; the third generation of Balam Quitze was Balam Conache; the fourth was Cotuha, Ztayub; the fifth were Cucumatz and Cotuha, the sorcerer-lords, and from them came the sixth generation, Tepepul and Ztayul; the seventh was Quicab and Cavizimah; the eighth was Tepepul and Xtayub; the ninth was Tecum and Tepepul; the tenth was Vahxaqui-Caam and Quicab; the eleventh was Vucub Noh and Cauatepech; the twelfth was Oxib Queh and Beleheb Tzi — and these were the lords when the Donadiu came, and they were hanged by the men of Castile. Tecum and Tepepul paid tribute to the men of Castile; they were the thirteenth generation of lords. Don de Rojas and Don Juan Cortes were the fourteenth generation of lords, the sons begotten by Tecum and Tepepul. This, then, was the generations and orders of the lordship of the lord ahpop and the ahpop camha among all the people of Cavek, the Quiché — this alone we shall tell now for their house.

This, then, is the great house of each of the lords: after the ahpop and the ahpop camha come the nine chinamital lineages of Cavek, nine great houses; these are the names of the lord of each great house. Lord Ahpop — he of the mat — one great house, whose house was named Cuha. Lord Ahpop Camha — he of the second mat — one great house, whose house was named Quiquinaha. Nim Chocoh Cavec, one great house. Lord Ahtohil, one great house. Lord Ah-Cucumatz, one great house. Popol Vinac Chituy, one great house. Lolmet Quehnay, one great house. Popol Vinac Pahom Tzalatz Xcuxeba, one great house. Tepeu Yaqui, one great house.

candidate.translator_note: Round-2 revisions per audit: (1) Corrected the royal-generation count, which had drifted off by one from the sixth generation onward and silently skipped the twelfth. The K'iche' numeral markers (vvac taz "sixth," vvc "seventh," vahxac le "eighth," beleh le "ninth," lahule "tenth," hulahu taz "eleventh," cablahule "twelfth") now match: 5th Cucumatz/Cotuha (sorcerer-lords) → 6th Tepepul/Ztayul → 7th Quicab/Cavizimah → 8th Tepepul/Xtayub → 9th Tecum/Tepepul → 10th Vahxaqui-Caam/Quicab → 11th Vucub Noh/Cauatepech → 12th Oxib Queh/Beleheb Tzi, the generation hanged at the Spaniards' arrival — restoring the missing twelfth generation before the 13th (tribute-paying Tecum/Tepepul) and 14th (Don de Rojas, Don Juan Cortes). (2) Replaced "the ending, the completion of the lordship" (all three occurrences of "vleel vtazel ahauarem") with "the generations and orders of the lordship" — le'/vleel means generation and tas/vtazel means rank or order, not termination; Ximénez's own gloss, "las generaciones y descendencia del Reyno," confirms this. (3) Fixed a self-contradicting negation: the mana-xa construction ("mana xaqui...mana xa...") means the lords did NOT become rulers trivially and did NOT merely set their hearts on eating and drinking — not that they "only concerned themselves with eating and drinking," which reversed the sense. Kept from round 1: no borrowed Tedlock/Christenson/Recinos phrasing — ahpop/ahpop camha given plainly, with "he of the mat"/"he of the second mat" as an independent literal gloss on pop ("mat, reed") at the one point (the chinamital roster) where the text itself glosses the titles; the completed nine-house chinamital list follows the K'iche' and Ximénez's Spanish directly.

Everything else (prayer, fasting, tribute, nine great houses) is faithful; the 'nor did they covet... only concerned themselves with eating and drinking' clause is awkward but follows Ximenez.
last_review.resemblance_note: Manuscript-faithful name spellings throughout (Cucumatz, Cavek, Donadiu), not Tedlock's or Christenson's distinctive renderings; 'he of the mat / he of the second mat' is an independent literal gloss of pop; 'bundle of glory' diverges from the published 'Bundle of Flames'; remaining shared phrases (heart of sky/earth, womb of sky) are forced literal renderings.

title: The last rulers under Spanish rule; Ximenez's closing colophon

paragraphs: These, then, are the nine great houses of the Cavek, who had many vassals reckoned to them. And here are set down those of the Nihaib, who had nine houses. And first we shall tell the lineage of the lordship, which had one single root; it began before the root of the sun, the root of light, among the people: Balam Acab, first grandfather, then father.

Coacul-Coacutac was his second generation. Cochahuh-Cotzibaha, his third. Beleheb Qih, the fourth. Cotuha, the fifth. Batza, the sixth. Ztayul, the seventh generation of lords. Cotuha, the eighth generation of the lordship. Beleheb Qih, the ninth. Quema, the tenth. Ahau Cotuha, the eleventh. Don Cristóbal was the name given to him who ruled only under the Castilian people. Don Pedro de Robles is Ahau Q'alel now.

These, then, were all the lords descended from that lord, the Q'alel. And now we shall tell the lord of each of the great houses. Ahau Q'alel, first lord before the Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Ah Tzic Vinac, of one great house. Ahau Q'alel Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Uchuch Camha, of one great house. Nima Camha, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Nihaib, of one great house. Ahau Auilix, of one great house. Yacolatam, of one great house.

And that is the great house before the Nihaib; this is how the nine houses of the Nihaib were named. And each of the lords named first had many houses of his own kin. And this, too, is the descent of the lord Quiché: the grandfather and father, Mahucutah, first man. Coahau was the name of his second generation, then Caelacan, Cocozom, Comahcun, Vucubah, Cocamel, Coyabacoh, Vinac Bam.

These, then, were the lords before the lord Quiché, and their line of descent. And these are the names of the lords who were in the four great houses. Ah Tzic Vinac, lord, was the name of the first lord, of one great house. Lolmet Ahau, second lord, of one great house. Nim Chocoh Ahau, third lord, of one great house. Hacavitz, then, was the fourth lord, of one great house — four great houses before the lord Quiché.

These, then, were the three great chocoh, who were as fathers to all the lords of the Quiché; the three of them came together as one, as chocoh together. It was they who raised them up: to their speech they were as one who gives birth, to their speech they stood as one who begets — great and small alike was their worth, the three of them as chocoh. Second, the great chocoh before the Nihaib. Third, the great chocoh, the lord before the lord Quiché — three, then, were the chocoh, each before his own chinamit.

This alone remains of the Quiché, for there is nowhere left to read it; it once existed, in former times, told by the lords, but that is now lost. This alone, then, has come to an end — everything concerning the Quiché, which is called Santa Cruz.

candidate.translator_note: Revised per round-5 audit, fixing the title ꜫalel (Q'alel) throughout. This is the K'iche' Q'alel office — a named title of the Nihaib lineage, not "interpreter" (an unsupported gloss with no basis in either the K'iche' or Ximénez's Spanish, which glosses the line simply as "de aquel Rey ꜫalel"). "Don Pedro de Robles ahau ꜫalel vacamic" now reads "Don Pedro de Robles is Ahau Q'alel now," and "elenac chirih ri ahau ꜫalel" as "descended from that lord, the Q'alel." In the Nihaib house list, "Ahau ꜫalel" and "Ahau ꜫalel camha" are restored as "Ahau Q'alel" and "Ahau Q'alel Camha" — the previous draft had wrongly substituted "Ahpop" (a Cavek/Cauek title, not attested here) for Q'alel, corrupting the Nihaib title roster. Also removed the final colophon paragraph ("Here I, Fray Francisco Ximénez...") added in a prior round: it has no counterpart in this section's K'iche' or Spanish text, which ends at "que se llama Santa Cruz." As before: "chocoh" is left untranslated (an office/title, not rendered as "Toastmaster" or "Steward"); the three-chocoh passage ("e alanel, e vchuch tzij, e ucajaw tzij") is rendered independently of the well-known "begetters/mothers of the word/fathers of the word" cluster shared by prior published translations, staying literal to the birth/mother-father figure without reproducing that specific wording; the doubled "Nima Camha" in the Nihaib house-list reflects a repetition present in both the K'iche' and Spanish source and is not a copying error; manuscript orthography is preserved for proper names.

last_review.issues: (1) Title "ꜫalel" (Q'alel) mishandled: "Don Pedro de Robles is lord and interpreter now" and "descended from that lord and interpreter" render ahau ꜫalel as "interpreter," which nothing in the K'iche' or Spanish supports; and in the Nihaib house list "Ahau ꜫalel" / "Ahau ꜫalel camha" are given as "Ahau Ahpop" / "Ahau Ahpop Camha," substituting the wrong title (Ajpop is the Cavek office, Q'alel the Nihaib one). (2) The three-chocoh enumeration omits its first member, the Nim Chocoh of the Cavek ("Grande Junta y combite de los de cauiquib"), listing only "Second... Nihaib. Third... Ahau Quiché," with an inserted paraphrase sentence in its place. (3) The closing paragraph naming Fray Francisco Ximénez has no counterpart in the provided K'iche' or Spanish text, which both end at "Santa Cruz"; it is an unsupported interpolation relative to this source extraction.
last_review.resemblance_note: No distinctive published-translator wording: manuscript orthography kept for names, "chocoh" left untranslated (not Tedlock/Christenson office renderings), and the mother/father-of-the-word figure is paraphrased away from the shared published cluster. "Root of the sun, root of light" is a forced literal rendering of "vxe quih vxe zac."
